---
title: "Exponential"
description: "A long right tail recedes slowly"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("../R/populations.R")
source("../R/diagnostics.R")
source("../R/simulation.R")
source("../R/plots.R")
library(ggplot2)
population <- get_population("exponential")
diagnostics <- read.csv("../results/diagnostics.csv")
page_results <- diagnostics[diagnostics$population == "exponential", ]
bands <- read.csv("../results/calibration_bands.csv")
second_seed <- read.csv("../results/second_seed.csv")
selected_n <- c(30, 300, 1000)
simulation <- simulate_population(population, selected_n, B = 10000L, seed = 631L, keep_means = TRUE)
```

## 1. Question and prediction

The Exponential parent is continuous but strongly right-skewed. I expected the ordinary CLT to work, yet much more slowly than for the symmetric die because averaging must tame a long right tail.

## 2. Parent population

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-parent
#| fig-cap: "The rate-1 Exponential density concentrates near zero and extends to the right. This asymmetry is the feature averaging must overcome."
#| fig-alt: "A density curve highest at zero and decreasing with a long right tail."
plot_parent_population(population)
```

## 3. Theory before simulation

For $X_i \sim Exp(1)$, $E(X)=1$ and $Var(X)=1$. All ordinary CLT conditions hold, giving center 1 and theoretical standard error $1/\sqrt{n}$.

The exact sample sum is Gamma, so the remaining standardized skewness shrinks like $2/\sqrt{n}$. This predicts slow but steady progress.

## 4. Simulation design

The adaptive grid extends from $n=1$ to $n=2000$, with extra points from 300 onward where shape diagnostics approach the practical bands. Every point uses 10,000 means and seed 631.

## 5. Numerical evidence

```{r}
#| label: tbl-exponential-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Exponential diagnostics near the transition. Center and SE are accurate before the right-tail shape meets the practical skewness guidance."
shown <- page_results[page_results$n %in% c(200, 300, 500, 750, 1000, 1500), c("n", "mean_error", "relative_se_error", "skewness", "excess_kurtosis", "qq_rmse")]
names(shown) <- c("n", "Center error", "Relative SE error", "Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q RMSE")
knitr::kable(shown, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

At $n=300$, skewness is `r sprintf("%.3f", page_results$skewness[page_results$n == 300])`, but the theoretical value $2/\sqrt{300}=0.115$ still exceeds the 0.10 guidance. A second seed also produces substantially more skew at 300 and 500, so the first run alone would give a premature threshold.

## 6. Shape across sample sizes

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-sampling
#| fig-cap: "At n = 30 the right tail is visible, and n = 300 remains borderline. By n = 1000 the histogram closely follows its dark theoretical Normal overlay under both theoretical and simulation checks."
#| fig-alt: "Three histograms centered near one, with right skew diminishing toward a dark Normal curve as sample size grows."
plot_sampling_distributions(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 7. Q-Q evidence

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-qq
#| fig-cap: "Right-tail Q-Q curvature is material at n = 30, still detectable at n = 300, and small at n = 1000. The comparison shows why a tail diagnostic delays the conclusion."
#| fig-alt: "Three Q-Q panels with decreasing upward curvature in the right tail."
plot_qq_comparison(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 8. Diagnostic trajectory

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Shape diagnostics generally decline with n but fluctuate under finite simulation. The sparse log-axis labels avoid implying a smooth monotone path, and the red lines show the Normal-calibrated guidance."
#| fig-alt: "Three line charts with declining skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q error over a log sample-size axis."
plot_diagnostic_trajectory(page_results, population, bands)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-se
#| fig-cap: "Empirical and theoretical standard errors agree long before the shape becomes convincingly Normal. Correct precision alone would certify the approximation too early."
#| fig-alt: "Two nearly overlapping standard-error curves declining with Exponential sample size."
plot_se_comparison(page_results, population)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-exponential-second-seed
#| tbl-cap: "Seed 1631 exposes the instability of n = 300 and 500, while n = 1000 is inside the skewness and Q-Q guidance under both seeds. Larger points confirm the same practical region despite Monte Carlo fluctuation."
seed_compare <- merge(
  page_results[page_results$n %in% second_seed$n, c("n", "skewness", "qq_rmse")],
  second_seed[, c("n", "skewness", "qq_rmse")],
  by = "n",
  suffixes = c("_631", "_1631")
)
names(seed_compare) <- c("n", "Skewness, seed 631", "Q-Q RMSE, seed 631", "Skewness, seed 1631", "Q-Q RMSE, seed 1631")
knitr::kable(seed_compare, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

## 9. Decision and disagreement

**Decision: use $n=1000$ as the conservative threshold.** The region from 750 to 1000 is where the practical shape becomes credible, but $n=300$ and 500 are seed-sensitive. At 1000, skewness and Q-Q RMSE are inside the guidance bands for both seeds, the dark Normal overlay and Q-Q line agree closely, and the primary-seed conclusion persists at $n=1500$ and 2000. Q-Q fluctuation at seed 1631 and $n=1500$ remains visible rather than being hidden.

## 10. Limitation and surprise

A single threshold cannot serve every tail probability. The most useful surprise is how early the mean and SE look correct compared with the shape: first and second moments alone would have declared victory much too soon.
